name: Standard Route
prior_findings: Mixes three approach lines (Hayden Pass, Dose Meadows/Lost Pass, Obstruction Pt/Grand Pass); the Grand Pass-to-summit prose heads the wrong direction. Rewrite around one line.

earlier_research.evidence: The peak has at least three documented ways in, and the row mixes them. An encyclopedia entry gives the easiest route as class 2 via the Hayden Pass Trail (matching the 1920 first-ascent line along the barrier ridge near Hayden Pass, i.e. pitch_detail); another summary describes Dose Meadows to Lost Pass (0.9-1 mi, 1,000-1,500 ft) or a high traverse from Obstruction Point over Grand Pass and Cameron Pass into the Lost River basin. No two independent sources establish which is THE standard line, and the Obstruction Point approach prose also runs cross-country east-northeast from the Cameron Creek basin, the wrong direction for a peak lying south of Grand Pass and southwest of Cameron. Making the row agree means rewriting approach, descent, descent_text, pitch_detail, beta, trailheadDirection and the waypoints around one chosen line, which is beyond a minimal researched patch.

earlier_research.correct_value: Obstruction Point Road: about 7.8-8 miles of narrow gravel from the Hurricane Ridge visitor area to the road-end trailhead
earlier_research.evidence: The route's trailhead card, approach, waypoints and itinerary all start at Obstruction Point, and road.name/status/seasonalGate describe Obstruction Point Road; only driveNote describes the Dosewallips washout (a different road on the south side). Two sources give Obstruction Point Road as a roughly 7.8-8 mile narrow gravel road leaving just below the Hurricane Ridge visitor center parking and ending at the Obstruction Point parking area.

earlier_research.fact: Route from Grand Pass to the summit and back
earlier_research.evidence: Tied to the approach-line dispute: the Grand Pass Trail continues from Grand Pass down Cameron Creek to Cameron Basin and over Cameron Pass into the Lost River basin, from which Lost Pass and Claywood are reached, so the itinerary/descent/waypoint version (Cameron Pass, Lost Basin, Lost Pass) is geographically coherent while the approach/descent_text version (direct cross-country ENE from the basin below Grand Pass, ~4-5 mi round trip beyond the pass) points the wrong way and understates the distance. No two independent sources describe the Obstruction Point line to Claywood in enough detail to write replacement prose safely.

Depends on which approach line the row adopts (Lost Basin below Lost Pass from the north, or Dose Meadows from the south); the Upper Cameron Basin pin sits on the other side of Cameron Pass. The bivy entries are owned by the separate camping clean-up and are not patched here; the itinerary/waypoint camp cannot be settled without first settling the approach line.

earlier_research.correct_value: A few hundred feet of net gain (6,150 to ~6,450-6,488 ft) but roughly 1,900-2,000 ft of total climbing to Grand Pass
earlier_research.evidence: The trailhead (6,150 ft) and Grand Pass (about 6,450 ft) differ by only ~300 ft, so '1,300 ft of net gain' is impossible. One hiking guide gives 4.3 mi/900 ft gain (1,650 ft loss) to Gladys Lake then 1.6 mi/1,000 ft to the pass, ~1,900 ft total climbing in ~5.9 mi; a second gives Gladys Lake to the pass as 1.5 mi/1,000 ft and the 12-mile out-and-back as 4,070 ft of gain, i.e. roughly 2,000 ft each way.

earlier_research.correct_value: Wilderness permit reserved in advance (no trailhead self-registration); bear canister required
earlier_research.evidence: The park's wilderness reservations page states paper self-registration permits are no longer available at trailheads; permits come through the federal reservation system, by phone, or in person at a Wilderness Information Center, and bear canisters are required in all wilderness camp areas. A second overview of Olympic permits repeats that trailhead self-registration is not available.

earlier_research.correct_value: ONP wilderness permit required for any overnight stay; Grand and Badger Valleys on the Obstruction Point approach are the quota area; canisters required in all wilderness camps
earlier_research.evidence: The park's quota list includes Royal Basin/Royal Lake and, separately, Grand and Badger Valleys; Royal Basin is a different drainage with no connection to this route, while Grand Valley lies on the Obstruction Point approach. Bear canisters are required in all wilderness camp areas, not only Royal Basin. A second source lists Grand Valley among the park's high-demand permit areas.

earlier_research.fact: Route from Grand Pass to the summit and back
earlier_research.evidence: The row describes three different approaches: Obstruction Point/Grand Pass cross-country (approach, descent_text, climbing_route), a Lost Basin camp via Cameron Pass and Lost Pass (itinerary, descent, timing), and Dosewallips to Dose Meadows/Lost Pass or Hayden Pass (beta, pitch_detail). No two independent sources describing the Obstruction Point line to Claywood were found on retry, and making the row agree would mean rewriting several prose fields rather than a minimal fix. Would be settled by choosing one approach line and finding two route descriptions of it (e.g. Dosewallips to Lost Pass, which is the best-documented line).

dist_km (17.3 km = 10.75 mi) is the one-way figure and is exactly half of the ~21.5 mi round trip in the itinerary total note and descent text; the itinerary days also sum to 21.5 mi. One-way vs round trip is the rendered convention (Approach (one way)), so the fields agree.

earlier_research.correct_value: A multi-day trip built around a basin camp, not a single day
earlier_research.evidence: The itinerary (3 days), its total note, the overview ('the approach itself is a multi-day undertaking'), beta, timing breakdown and partner requirements all treat this as multi-day; only descent_text offers a single long day. An Obstruction Point to Dose Meadows through-hiker trip report shows the Grand Pass / Cameron Pass / Lost Pass leg alone (about 11 mi with three passes) took a full day, so a round trip to Claywood beyond Lost Pass is not a realistic single day.

The Cameron Pass pin (47.9485, -123.2591) does sit far northeast of both Grand Pass and the summit, but pin coordinates are out of scope for this pass and no patch is written. Settling it needs a pin-repair pass using the pass's mapped coordinate.

earlier_research.correct_value: Jefferson County (peak and rescue county)
earlier_research.evidence: Wikipedia and PeakVisor both place Mount Claywood in Jefferson County, inside Olympic National Park. Washington law (RCW 38.52.400) makes the chief law enforcement officer of the political subdivision (the county sheriff) responsible for local search and rescue, so the county SAR named in the notes should be Jefferson, matching emergency.county.

row.overview: Mount Claywood (6,836 ft) sits at the head of the Lost River in Olympic National Park's interior, about 2.4 mi southwest of taller Mount Cameron (7,190 ft) and roughly 15 mi east of Mount Olympus, with Mt. Fromme just 0.58 mi to its southeast. Lt. Joseph P. O'Neil named it "Mount Clay Wood" in 1885 to honor his commanding officer, Col. Henry Clay Wood — this peak marked the deepest northern penetration of O'Neil's 1885 Olympic exploration expedition. Runoff drains north/west into the Elwha River and east via Claywood Lake to the Dosewallips River. There is no maintained trail to the summit; it is reached only by a long cross-country push beyond Cameron Basin, making it one of the more rarely-climbed named peaks in the park's interior.
row.beta: Claywood has no maintained summit trail. Parties approach via the Dosewallips River Trail to Dose Meadows, then climb the short but very steep unmaintained path to Lost Pass (5,570 ft) on the ridge between Lost Peak and Claywood, and finally leave the trail entirely for a cross-country scramble over talus, heather benches, and loose rock to the 6,836 ft summit. It is almost always combined with neighboring Lost Peak, Mount Fromme, and/or Sentinel Peak from a single Dose Meadows or Lost Pass camp, since the approach itself is a multi-day undertaking.
row.permit: Olympic National Park: no permit for day climbs; all overnight wilderness stays require a wilderness camping permit via Recreation.gov.
row.comms: No reliable cell coverage in the Dosewallips valley, at Hayden Pass, or on the barrier ridge — Olympic National Park's backcountry has limited-to-no service outside park headquarters/visitor centers; carry a satellite communicator or PLB and file a trip plan with someone outside the park.
row.descent: Reverse the ascent line back down into the Lost River drainage and up to Cameron Pass, then out via the Cameron Pass and Grand Pass Trails to Obstruction Point. Loose, chossy rock on the upper mountain (typical of this interior Olympic massif) warrants care while downclimbing, especially in descending light or wet conditions.

row.best_season: Late July through September is the realistic window: Obstruction Point Road (the standard approach road) typically doesn't open until mid-July, and snow can linger on the Cameron Pass approach and Claywood's upper, shaded slopes well into midsummer, so an ice axe is worth carrying even in July.
row.approach: From the Obstruction Point Trailhead (6,150 ft) — reached via the narrow, unpaved Obstruction Point Road that branches off Hurricane Ridge Road just below Hurricane Ridge — follow the Grand Pass Trail as it climbs onto and traverses Lillian Ridge. The first mile-plus is an easy, open ridge walk (the unmarked boot path up the Lillian Ridge Way / Elk Mountain high route splits off here for those doing the ridge-top variation instead). The trail then drops into the Grand Lake basin before climbing steadily to Grand Pass (6,488 ft) at roughly 5.95 mi and only a few hundred feet of net gain from the trailhead but close to 2,000 ft of total climbing, because the trail first loses well over 1,000 ft into the lake basin. Seasonal tarns in the Grand Lake basin below the pass are the last reliable water before the climb to the pass — fill up there, since water on the open ridge is unreliable. From Grand Pass the maintained trail ends for this objective: the route to Claywood's summit continues cross-country, dropping a few hundred feet down loose scree and shale on the pass's east side into the upper Cameron Creek/Lillian Basin drainage (moderately steep and loose underfoot, worse when wet — this gully is the one approach-specific hazard called out by parties doing this same descent off Grand Pass in trip reports). From the basin floor, contour and climb generally east-northeast across open alpine benches and talus toward the Cameron–Claywood divide, staying below Mount Cameron's north ridge and aiming for the shoulder immediately west/southwest of Claywood's summit block (Claywood's nearest higher neighbor, Mount Cameron, sits about 2.4 mi northeast; Mt. Fromme and Sentinel Peak are just southeast of Claywood in the same cluster). The final several hundred feet to the 6,836 ft summit are class 2–3 scrambling on broken shale and loose scree — similar in character to the well-documented scramble route on neighboring Lost Peak in the same basin system. This whole cross-country stretch beyond Grand Pass (roughly 4–5 mi round trip of the route's total ~21.5 mi) is unmarked, off-trail, and route-finding is real: bring a topo/GPS track and only attempt it with good visibility, since the terrain is used almost exclusively by peak-baggers linking Claywood with Cameron, Fromme, Lost, and Sentinel rather than by any constructed path.
row.descent_text: This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappelling is involved. From the summit, reverse the class 2–3 scramble down to the shoulder on the Cameron–Claywood divide, then descend back into the upper Cameron Creek/Lillian Basin drainage on the same talus and open benches used on the way up. Regain Grand Pass by climbing the loose scree/shale slope on the basin's west side; this slope is notably looser and more insecure on the reascent than it felt going down, so expect slow, careful travel with some hand use, and glissadeable snow patches here in early season instead. From Grand Pass, follow the Grand Pass Trail back over Lillian Ridge to the Obstruction Point Trailhead. Watch for afternoon thunderstorm buildup over the exposed ridge on the final miles, and budget real time for the cross-country middle section in both directions — at roughly 21.5 mi / 34.6 km round trip with a significant off-trail component, this is a trip built around a basin camp rather than a single day, and parties should reverse-navigate carefully rather than assume the outbound track is easy to retrace.

climate.spring: Snow lingers at Hayden Pass and on the barrier ridge well into early summer; the pass typically doesn't melt out until mid-July.

climate.winter: Heavy, wet snowfall and elevated avalanche danger in the Olympic high country; the approach road/trail is not maintained or plowed.
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate: Pacific frontal systems are forced upward over the Olympics (orographic lift), producing high precipitation, especially heavy winter snowfall that can linger at these elevations into midsummer.

approach_variants.notes: A long valley walk to Dose Meadows, then the unmaintained Lost Pass path — under a mile and over a thousand feet of climbing, steep and rooty the whole way. Grand Pass from the Obstruction Point side reaches the same high country from the north over Lillian Ridge and down loose shale into the upper Cameron drainage. Either way this is normally linked with Lost Peak, Fromme or Sentinel from one camp.

approach_variants.baseFinding: Lost Pass is the low notch on the ridge between Lost Peak and Claywood, reached by a steep unmaintained path climbing straight out of the meadows. Standing in the notch, the rounded summit immediately northeast is Lost Peak — that is the decoy, and it is where most parties who reach this pass actually go. Claywood is the higher, greyer, more broken mass across open ground to the southwest. Leave the notch and climb and traverse southwest over heather benches and talus toward the shoulder just west of the summit block. The base of the scrambling is where the heather gives out and the ground becomes broken shale plates and loose scree, with occasional cairns picking a line through short Class 3 steps. Fromme and Sentinel stand immediately southeast of Claywood in the same cluster and are separate summits, so do not settle for the first top you reach. If the ground you are on has started dropping toward Cameron Creek, you have crossed too far and should regain height on the divide.

climbing_route.label: Summit block from the west/southwest shoulder
climbing_route.notes: The final several hundred feet to the 6,836 ft summit are scrambling on broken shale and loose scree, from the shoulder immediately west/southwest of Claywood's summit block.

bivy.name: Dose Meadows
bivy.notes: The base for Mount Claywood, and the southern base for Mount Cameron by way of Lost Pass and Cameron Pass. It sits at about four thousand four hundred and seventy feet at the head of the Dosewallips, and the single fact that dominates any plan built around it is the road. The Dosewallips road has been cut by a washout for over two decades and is not being rebuilt, so you start with roughly five and a half miles of old roadbed before the trail proper, and the meadows are then somewhere around seventeen to nineteen miles from where you actually park. Bicycles are permitted on the roadbed as far as the old ranger station at the wilderness boundary, which removes a meaningful chunk of that and is worth the hassle of hauling a bike. Realistically this is a two-day approach each way for most parties, which puts Claywood firmly in the category of a four to five day objective rather than a weekend. The alternative doors are Gray Wolf Pass from the Gray Wolf river, or the long way round from Obstruction Point, and neither is short. Claywood itself has no established camp of its own: parties climb it from the meadows or bivouac wherever they get to on the ridge, and there is no designated high camp to book.
bivy.water: The infant Dosewallips river runs through the meadows. Reliable.
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required; not a quota area, so it is normally available. Standard per-permit reservation charge and per-adult nightly fee through the federal recreation booking system, and a hard-sided bear canister is required. There is no permit or fee for the road-walk section below the park boundary, but you do need somewhere legal to leave the car at the closure.
bivy.capacity: Several sites spread through the meadow area, plus stock use in season. It is a junction camp on a long loop, so it is rarely empty and rarely crowded.

bivy.name: Cameron Basin
bivy.notes: This is the working base for Mount Cameron, which is climbed from Cameron Pass just above the basin, and it is the western end of this zone rather than part of the Needles group at all. Two ways in and they are very different. From Obstruction Point it is a high, scenic and long day over Grand Pass and down into the basin, and it depends entirely on the Obstruction Point road, a rough high-elevation dirt road that typically does not open until well into July and closes with the first snow of autumn; if that road is shut, this approach does not exist. From the south it is reached from Dose Meadows over Lost Pass, which is short in distance and brutally steep, but getting to Dose Meadows means the whole washed-out Dosewallips walk first. Nothing about this camp helps you on The Needles, and a party trying to combine Cameron with Deception in one trip is really planning two trips. Snow lies late in the basin and on Cameron Pass, and the descent off Grand Pass wants a dry day.
bivy.water: Cameron Creek and its feeders through the basin. Reliable through the climbing season.
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required; Cameron Basin itself is not a quota area, so it books readily. The catch is the approach: if you come the sensible way from Obstruction Point you pass through Grand and Badger Valleys, which ARE a quota area with reservations in effect through the high summer, so a night at Grand or Moose Lake on the way in has to be booked separately and early. Bear canisters are required throughout. Everything is reserved through the federal recreation booking system with the standard per-permit charge and per-adult nightly fee.
bivy.capacity: Several backcountry sites in the basin below Cameron Pass. Modest but usually adequate; the basin is on a well-travelled loop, so summer weekends can be busier than the remoteness suggests.

row.name: Meade Glacier
hazards: Steep snowfield below the summit requires solid self-arrest skills.
Loose rock on the summit scramble creates rockfall risk for parties climbing close together.
The Conrad and Meade Glaciers are receding but can still harbor hidden crevasses/moats in early season.
Long, remote approach (~20 miles round trip) with limited water in late-season dry years.
row.overview: The standard/easiest ascent: a long approach through Conrad Meadows and over Klickton Divide, gaining the Meade Glacier's permanent snowfields on the peak's southeast side and finishing with a short class 3 scramble to the summit block.
row.beta: From the Conrad Meadows / South Fork Tieton Trailhead, follow Trail #1120 through Conrad Meadows and up toward Warm Lake, then traverse southwest to Klickton Divide and follow the ridge (mixing snow and rock, with Gilbert in view most of the way) toward the summit block. Alternatively, climbers can cross the east side of the Conrad Glacier to the saddle east of the summit, drop onto the Meade Glacier, and climb it (now largely reduced to persistent snowfields rather than a crevassed glacier) to a rock outcrop below the final pitch. Either way, the route tops out with a steep snow/scree slope and a short, loose class 3 scramble through a notch to the true summit. Very popular and rated the most straightforward line up the peak, though it is a long day (~20 miles round trip) with real elevation gain.
row.turnaround: Set a firm turnaround time before starting the final snow/scree slope and summit scramble — afternoon thunderstorms and softening, rockfall-prone snow are the main reasons to abandon the summit push and retreat the way you came.
row.permit: Free self-issue Goat Rocks Wilderness permit at trailheads and ranger stations; Northwest Forest Pass or day fee at several trailheads.
row.comms: Cell service is unreliable at the trailhead and throughout the wilderness; plan on having none past the trailhead.
row.descent: Reverse the ascent route down the summit scramble, the snowfield, and Klickton Divide back to Conrad Meadows Trail #1120.

row.best_season: Late June through October is climbable, but the route is very snow-dependent: early season (June-July) offers a firmer, more continuous snow climb up the Meade Glacier snowfields but requires crampons/ice axe and avalanche awareness; by late summer (Aug-Sept) the snow largely melts out, exposing a rougher boot path and looser rock on the final scramble; conditions vary significantly year to year with snowpack.
row.approach: Drive to the Conrad Meadows / South Fork Tieton Trailhead (Trail #1120, elev. ~4,044 ft): from Naches, WA take US-12 W about 22 miles, turn onto Forest Road 1200 (Tieton Reservoir Road) for 4.5 miles, then onto Forest Road 1000 (South Fork Tieton Road) for 12.6 miles to the trailhead at road's end (last ~7 miles gravel, generally in good condition). Hike Trail #1120 through Conrad Meadows (crossing Conrad Creek) into the Goat Rocks Wilderness, continuing toward Surprise Lake and Warm Lake, then climb southwest to gain Klickton Divide near Point 6,882 before following the ridge northwest toward the summit.
row.descent_text: From the summit, downclimb the same class 3 notch and steep snow/scree slope used on ascent, then follow Klickton Divide back southeast. Rejoin the boot path down through Warm Lake basin and Conrad Meadows to the trailhead. Many parties vary the return via Surprise Lake for scenery; glissading the snowfield below the summit is common in early/mid season when snow is consolidated (self-arrest gear required).
row.bail: The ridge/glacier approach has no major technical commitment below the final summit scramble — parties can retreat along Klickton Divide or back down the snowfield to Warm Lake/Conrad Meadows at essentially any point before the summit notch.

row.itinerary: Typically done as an overnight/2-day backpack: Day 1, hike in to a camp at Surprise Lake (wooded, sheltered) or Warm Lake (above treeline, exposed to wind); Day 2, alpine start for the summit push over Klickton Divide and the Meade Glacier snowfields, then return to camp and hike out (or split the hike-out over a 3rd day). Strong parties have done it car-to-car in a long single day.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July, while the Meade basin still holds continuous firm snow and before the steep summit snowfield thins over loose rubble

July.reason: The Meade basin is a continuous, firm snow climb with crampons, snowbridges still hold over creeks and moats, and camps near Conrad Creek have water.

June.reason: Road to Conrad Meadows is usually passable, but Conrad Creek runs high and deep snow makes the upper approach slow and avalanche-exposed.

August.reason: The basin usually still holds snow, but the steep snowfield below the summit scramble softens and thins, and moats open at the glacier edges.

October.reason: First storms put fresh snow on icy old snow and loose rock, days are short for a 20-mile round trip, and the approach road can close with early snow.

September.reason: Snow melts back to hard, thin patches over loose rubble with bad runouts, the summit scramble is looser, and water on the long approach gets scarce.

approach_variants.baseFinding:
GAINING KLICKTON DIVIDE IN THE RIGHT PLACE IS THE WHOLE ROUTE-FINDING PROBLEM, AND EVERYTHING BEFORE IT IS TRAIL.

You leave the trail beyond Warm Lake and climb SOUTHWEST to gain the divide near POINT 6,882. From there the ridge runs NORTHWEST to the peak. Two directions, in that order: southwest to gain, northwest to follow. Getting the second one wrong walks you away from the mountain along the same ridge.

THE POSITIVE THAT MAKES THIS A GENEROUS ROUTE IN CLEAR WEATHER, AND A HARSH ONE IN CLOUD: once you are on the divide, GILBERT IS IN VIEW ALMOST THE WHOLE WAY. If you cannot see the peak from the ridge you are either not on the divide or the day has closed in, and in the second case the ridge crest itself is the handrail.

THE BASE OF THE CLIMBING IS A NOTCH, AND THERE IS ONLY ONE. The route tops out with a steep snow and scree slope and then a SHORT, LOOSE CLASS 3 SCRAMBLE THROUGH A NOTCH to the true summit. Short is the operative word: the summit is immediately above the notch. If you have gone through a gap and the ground keeps rising well beyond it, you are at the wrong gap.

THE NEGATIVE THAT SEPARATES THIS FROM ITS SIBLING ON THE SAME PEAK: this line goes ONTO THE RIDGE. The other route from this trailhead goes UNDER the peak — across the east side of the Conrad Glacier to a saddle, then onto the Meade. If you find yourself roping up for glacier travel before you have been on a ridge, you are on that one instead.

SELF-ARREST IS PART OF THE BASE FINDING HERE, NOT AN AFTERTHOUGHT: the snowfield below the summit is steep enough that the route assumes you can hold a slip on it. Arriving without an axe is a reason to turn round at the divide.

bivy.name: Conrad Meadows and Surprise Lake, South Fork Tieton
bivy.notes: This is the correct side of the range for Gilbert Peak's Conrad Glacier and Meade Glacier routes, and there is no sensible way to reach either from the Snowgrass trailheads — the two approaches are separated by the whole crest. From the road end the trail runs level through meadows for around four miles before the loop divides, and the northern fork leads toward Surprise Lake and eventually the benches, waterfall and Barren Lake below the Conrad Glacier. Most parties camp once in the basin and climb from there, since the glacier and the traverse across the Meade to Gilbert's south ridge make for a long day on their own. The meadows at the road end are a legitimate first night if you arrive late, but they are low, buggy in early summer and a long way from anything. This side is far quieter than Snowgrass, and the corresponding cost is a much longer approach and much less traffic if something goes wrong.

bivy.permit: Free self-issued wilderness permit at the trailhead board once you cross into the wilderness. Camping is prohibited within 100 feet of lakes. Note this trailhead sits on the drier eastern forest rather than the Gifford Pinchot side, so confirm which parking pass the board is asking for before leaving the car. Heavy stock use means the meadows are shared with horse parties.
bivy.capacity: Primitive dispersed and stock camping in the broad meadows at the road end, and established backcountry sites at Surprise Lake several miles up the loop; no reservations and no numbered sites

row.overview: Pernod is the highest of the four Wine Spires (Burgundy, Chianti, Chablis, and Pernod) above Washington Pass. Fred Beckey, Dick McGowan, and Don Wilde made the first ascent in September 1952, an aid-heavy climb by today's standards: pitons for both protection and direct aid, a hand-drilled Rawl-drive bolt to protect an insecure section, another bolt to facilitate an 8-foot pendulum around an overhanging, holdless corner, and more bolts placed from a shoulder-stand to reach the summit. The modern route follows essentially the same line, reached via the long Burgundy Col approach.
row.beta: Per Beckey-guide-derived route descriptions, Pernod and neighboring Chablis are considered the easiest of the Wine Spires and can be climbed in an easy day; the climbing is moderate (5.5-5.7) and not sustained.

row.permit: No climbing or wilderness permit required; no Northwest Forest Pass is needed to park at the SR-20 roadside pullout used for this approach (the pass applies at developed trailheads elsewhere in the corridor).
row.descent: Descend via the standard descent route, retracing the ascent when possible. Be aware of loose rock and snow bridge hazards. Maintain group cohesion on exposed sections.

row.pro_needs: Solid alpine rock pro across the grade.
row.approach: From the roadside pullout on SR-20 about 0.7 mile past the Cutthroat Lake Road turnoff (directly across the highway from the Wine Spires), a boot/climbers' trail drops off the shoulder, crosses Early Winters Creek on logs or a rock-hop (can run high and require a wet ford in early-season snowmelt), and climbs a timbered rib on the climber's-left side of the Burgundy Creek drainage. The trail gains steeply and steadily — on the order of 2,000 ft over the first 1.5-2 miles — to a broad, flat bench at roughly 6,400-6,600 ft that holds established camps; this bench is the last reliable water (small tarns/creek trickle, can run dry by late summer — treat before drinking). From the bench, leave the main Burgundy Col trail and contour right past a couple of subsidiary buttresses, dropping slightly before regaining a large talus/scree gully that runs directly to the base of Pernod's west face. This final gully is loose scree-over-slab ('kitty litter,' Class 2-3) and is the route-finding and footing crux of the approach, especially under a pack — trekking poles help. All told the approach is roughly 3,500-4,000 ft of gain over about 3 miles one-way (3-5 hours for a fit party). Lingering snow in the gully into early July may require an axe/light traction for the last few hundred feet in a big-snow year; check current conditions before committing. Burgundy Col itself also holds 3-4 bivy sites (one large enough for a 2-person tent), with old rock wind-shelters built by past parties still standing.
row.descent_text: This is a rappel descent, not a walk-off. From the summit, the first rappel drops into the notch just below/east of the top — anchors on this line are natural (slung horns and blocks, occasional aging fixed webbing/tat) rather than bolted, so carry some cord to back up or replace sun-bleached slings. From the notch, continue down a further string of rappels on the peak's back (east) side into the Silver Star Glacier basin rather than reversing the approach gully; expect on the order of 4-5 rappels total to reach easy glacier snow/talus. A single 60m rope works but is tight in a few spots — many parties run a 70m single or rappel on doubled ropes so they're not left short above the next anchor — and watch for rope-stuck hazard pulling ropes through the blocky terrain. Once down on the Silver Star Glacier, climb/traverse back up a few hundred feet to regain Burgundy Col, then descend the standard climbers' trail (scree bench, then timbered rib) back to the SR-20 pullout, essentially reversing the approach. Rope up for the glacier crossing if there's any question about moat/crevasse conditions, and budget real time for the loose 'kitty litter' scree below the col — it's notoriously slow going.
row.bail: Rappel from any belay if forced to retreat.

pitch_detail.notes: Lower-angle rock gains the base of the technical climbing above the scree gully approach; easy ground used to reach the first real belay stance on the wall.
Moderate crack and corner climbing following essentially the same line the 1952 first-ascent party (Beckey, Wilde, McGowan) established, before the angle and difficulty pick up higher on the face.
Sustained face moves lead toward the route's historically hardest section; solid granite with adequate but spaced protection.
The insecure section the first-ascent party protected with a hand-drilled Rawl-drive bolt — the old fixed bolt (or its replacement) still marks the technical crux of the lower wall.

Passes the overhanging, holdless corner that stumped the 1952 first ascensionists, who bolted and pendulumed roughly 8 feet around it on aid; most modern parties free it near 5.9, though a short pull on gear (A0) remains an option if it doesn't go free.

Finishes at the small summit block using bolts the first-ascent trio placed from a shoulder-stand to reach the top; treat these old, weathered bolts with caution and back them up with gear/slings where possible before starting the multi-rappel descent.
pitch_detail.anchor: Old fixed bolts (summit, FA shoulder-stand aid points)

row.corrections: The given data listed only a route name ('Standard Rock Route') with no other detail. Cross-referencing the Beckey Cascade Alpine Guide description (surfaced via SummitPost's Chianti Spire page, which covers the Wine Spires as a group) and the 1952 AAJ first-ascent account, this route appears to correspond to Pernod's original, easiest line — 5.5-5.7, moderate and not sustained per the guidebook — established by Beckey, Wilde, and McGowan, distinct from the harder Direct West Face (5.10+) and the South Face (5.9 A0). I could not find a source giving this route's exact pitch count, current bolt condition, or a dedicated modern topo/rack beyond the historical FA account and guidebook summary — treat those specifics as unconfirmed until a current source is found. 2026-07-31: waypoints[0] (Burgundy Col) note replaced — previously a leaked internal-research artifact referencing "this session's own Vasiliki Tower research", not a real route note. rappel_detail.notes: Rappel from Pernod's true summit down the south face to a notch/ledge near Chablis Spire; a single 70m rope reaches, a 60m leaves you short of the notch.
rappel_detail.anchor: bolted (new bolt + old original 1/4-inch bolt with hanger, backed by 2 equalized pitons)

rappel_detail.notes: After a short 4th-class downclimb/scramble to regain Chablis Spire's east-face rap line, first of two double-rope rappels down that route toward its base.
Second double-rope rappel down Chablis Spire's east-face route, reaching the base of that route rather than descending directly into the Silver Star Glacier basin.

row.rappel_count_note: 1 rappel off the true summit on a bolted anchor down to a notch/ledge near Chablis Spire, then a short 4th-class scramble to regain Chablis's east-face rappel line, then 2 double-rope rappels down that line to the base.

approach_variants.name: The Wine Spires pullout and the bench camp, then contour right off the Burgundy Col trail into the gully under the west face
approach_variants.notes: From the roadside pullout on SR-20 about 0.7 mile past the Cutthroat Lake Road turnoff, directly across the highway from the Wine Spires, a boot and climbers' trail drops off the shoulder, crosses Early Winters Creek on logs or a rock-hop, and climbs a timbered rib on the climber's-left side of the Burgundy Creek drainage. The creek can run high and require a wet ford in early-season snowmelt. The trail gains steeply and steadily, on the order of 2,000 ft over the first 1.5-2 miles, to a broad flat bench at roughly 6,400-6,600 ft that holds established camps. THIS BENCH IS THE LAST RELIABLE WATER: small tarns and a creek trickle that can run dry by late summer. Roughly 3,500-4,000 ft of gain over about 3 miles one-way, 3-5 hours for a fit party. Note that the aspect recorded for this route says north while its own approach and descent describe the west face and an east-side rappel.
hazards: Loose scree-over-slab in the final approach gully, the footing crux of the day
Lingering snow in the gully into early July in a big-snow year
A rappel descent down the opposite side of the peak onto a glacier, followed by a re-ascent to Burgundy Col
Natural anchors only, with aging fixed webbing; carry cord to back up or replace
A single 60 m rope is tight in places on the descent; many parties run a 70 m or doubles
The bench is the last reliable water and can run dry by late summer
approach_variants.baseFinding:
LEAVE THE MAIN BURGUNDY COL TRAIL AT THE BENCH. THAT IS THE TURN, AND MISSING IT IS THE ONLY WAY TO GET THIS APPROACH WRONG. From the bench, contour RIGHT past a couple of subsidiary buttresses, DROPPING SLIGHTLY before regaining a large talus and scree gully that runs directly to the base of Pernod's west face.

SO THERE IS A SMALL DESCENT IN THE MIDDLE OF AN OTHERWISE RELENTLESS CLIMB, AND THAT DIP IS THE CONFIRMATION. If everything you have done since the bench has been uphill, you are still on the Burgundy Col trail.

THE GULLY IS THE ROUTE-FINDING AND FOOTING CRUX OF THE APPROACH: loose scree over slab, class 2-3, described as kitty litter, especially under a pack. Trekking poles help. Lingering snow in it into early July may require an axe or light traction for the last few hundred feet in a big-snow year.

ARRIVAL: the base of Pernod's west face, THE TALLEST WALL IN THE WINE SPIRES. Six pitches at Grade III. If the wall above you is one of the smaller buttresses you passed on the contour, you stopped too early.

AND FOR PARTIES WHO CAMP HIGH INSTEAD: Burgundy Col itself holds three or four bivy sites, one large enough for a two-person tent, with old rock wind-shelters built by past parties still standing. Those shelters are a positive identification of the col.

DESCENT IS BY RAPPEL DOWN THE BACK, NOT BY REVERSING THE APPROACH GULLY: the first rappel drops into the notch just below and east of the top, then a string of rappels continues down the peak's EAST side into the Silver Star Glacier basin, on the order of four to five in total. Anchors are natural, slung horns and blocks with occasional aging fixed webbing, not bolts. Once on the glacier, climb back up a few hundred feet to regain Burgundy Col, then descend the standard climbers' trail.

bivy.name: Burgundy Col high camp — WEST side, the Wine Spires
bivy.notes: The narrow saddle between Burgundy Spire and the ridge, and the standard high camp for the Wine Spires and for the Silver Star Glacier approached from the highway side. Published elevations disagree by a couple of hundred feet, with figures from roughly 7,720 to 7,950 in circulation, so treat any single number as approximate. It is exposed to wind from both sides and several parties have dropped back down the west slope to sleep after a rough night. Camping here removes about 1,500 ft of the scree from summit day, which is most of the argument for carrying overnight gear up it.
bivy.water: No spring or stream. Parties melt snow from the lingering patches on the glacier side of the col, which normally hold into late summer but can be rock-hard in the morning or gone entirely in a dry, late season. Many simply haul all their water up the scree, which is the single heaviest decision on this approach.
bivy.permit: None. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any designated wilderness — no quota, no reservation and no self-issue permit, unlike the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
bivy.capacity: Two to four rock-ringed bivy platforms; roughly one is level enough for a two-person tent, so a large party should expect to sleep scattered or send some members back down

bivy.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — WEST side
bivy.notes: The flat, sheltered alternative to sleeping at the col, in trees before the timbered rib gives way to open scree. Reports consistently call it the more pleasant camp of the two, at the cost of extra vertical on summit morning. Elevation is quoted anywhere from about 6,400 to 6,500 ft depending on which flat spot a party used. Its value is almost entirely the spring: if that has failed, the bench loses most of its advantage over the col.
bivy.water: The most dependable water on this approach, but NOT from the obvious place. The creek shown on maps immediately east of the bench is frequently dry, while a spring roughly ten minutes north of camp keeps running well into September in most years. Confirm it before committing, and expect insects around it.
bivy.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, non-wilderness, so no permit or reservation applies.
bivy.capacity: Several established tent spots on a wooded bench, with a large boulder and an old fire ring as the usual landmark; comfortably three or four tents

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground, SR 20
bivy.notes: A roadside vehicle campground rather than a site on any approach — it is for sleeping the night before, not for the climb. It opens around May and closes with the first serious snow, tracking the same window as everything else here. The whole area is gated by the SR 20 winter closure, which shuts in late November or early December and reopens in spring, with the date driven by avalanche work and storm damage rather than the calendar. In closed months the pullout is inside the gated section and the approach becomes a long ski or snowmobile trip.
bivy.water: No drinking water at the campground. Early Winters Creek runs alongside and needs filtering; Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds, farther east, have drinking water in season.
bivy.permit: Per-night campground fee; no wilderness permit involved. The unmarked Silver Star Creek pullout that starts the west approach is not itself a signed fee site — check current signage rather than assuming either way.
bivy.capacity: 27 developed first-come, first-served sites for tents and small vehicles

bivy.name: Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — WEST side
bivy.notes: Not an established campsite so much as a fallback for a party that has run out of daylight or water partway up the talus. The main reason to know about them is that the water situation on this hillside is patchy rather than uniform, so a dry creek at the wooded bench does not necessarily mean a dry mountainside above it. Anyone counting on this should carry a stove and be prepared to find nothing.
bivy.water: Genuinely unreliable and conditions-dependent. At least one party found a trickle running here in a season when the bench camp creek below was dry, which makes it worth checking on the way up, but nothing about it is dependable enough to plan a camp around.
bivy.permit: None. Non-wilderness National Forest land; no permit, quota or registration.
bivy.capacity: Improvised, one or two small parties at most; flat ground has to be found or built rather than chosen

earlier_research.fact: Which col separates Little Sister from Cinderella
earlier_research.correct_value: The 6,240+ ft col southeast of the summit is the Cinderella-Little Sister col (the Southeast Ridge's start).
earlier_research.evidence: Cinderella Peak sits at 48.69092,-121.97156, east-southeast of Little Sister (48.69241,-121.97649), and the Southeast Ridge is described as beginning at the col between Cinderella and Little Sister above the looker's-left (south) side of the glacier. The 2015 winter party went up snow to the col east of Little Sister (6240+ ft, southeast of the summit) and wrapped round to the south side. So the variant's claim that the Cinderella col lies northwest/west is wrong. (Note: the Southeast Ridge row's baseFinding says other routes on the peak do not go to the col, which this route does - a cross-row issue, not patched here.)

row.name: South Couloir
row.fa: Unknown (first known ski descent: Mark Allen, May 2007)
hazards: Steep snow/ice couloir terrain (up to ~50 degrees).
Two rappels on the descent, from anchors you build yourself.
Remote and rarely climbed — rescue access would be very limited.
row.overview: A steep snow/ice/mixed couloir on Little Sister's south side, called out in a 2007 account of the first known ski traverse of the entire Twin Sisters Range as 'the proudest line of the trip.'
row.beta: This line was skied as part of a multi-day (May 12-14) south-to-north ski traverse of the Twin Sisters Range by Chris Simmons, Mark Allen, Greg Balco, and Paul Kimbrough. On the second day one of them skied Little Sister's South Couloir, singled out as the trip's best line. The traverse's technical crux - about 40 m of 4th-class rock, 100+ m of 50-degree ice, then 100+ m of rappelling ending in a fixed rappel with a knot pass - came later, on a crossing of the range near South Twin Sister, not on this peak.
row.turnaround: Set a hard turnaround before you leave the car and honor it, because the retreat from this peak is dominated by the six-hour walk out, not by the climbing. Work backwards from the log crossing: you want to be back at the Middle Fork with enough margin that a dark or wet crossing is optional rather than forced. Reassess at the 6,240+ ft col — if you are not there with several hours of usable light in hand, the summit is not worth the exit. Treat softening south-facing snow as its own clock: once the slope you climbed on firm neve is punching through, the descent is slower and the avalanche picture is changing, and that is a reason to go down regardless of what the watch says.
row.rappels: Two rappels on the descent. One party made a double-60 m rappel from near the top of the line and a second rappel down from the col southeast of the summit; they noted a single 60 m rope would have been enough for the col rappel. Anchors are not fixed — bring cord and tat, and expect to build off rock horns or leave a picket/screw.
row.face: South side of Little Sister, above the 6,240+ ft col that separates it from Cinderella Peak
row.permit: No climbing permit; parking at the Elbow Lake Trailhead needs a Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass.
row.comms: No sourced cell-coverage data exists for this peak. Assume no service on the drive up FR 38, none at the trailhead, and none in the Middle Fork Nooksack valley or the forested Green Creek approach — the valley is deep and screened from the Puget lowlands. Carry a satellite messenger or PLB and leave a detailed itinerary with someone who will actually call it in. Whatcom County Search and Rescue is activated through 911.
row.descent: Reverse the line: downclimb and rappel the gully, then descend south-side snow back to the col and reverse the Green Creek approach.

waypoints.name: Elbow Lake Trailhead (FR 38, Middle Fork Nooksack)

timing.recommendedStart: Early morning from the trailhead. The documented winter ascent left the cars at 7:10 a.m. and still finished after dark; in spring, start pre-dawn to reach the south-facing couloir while the snow is still firm and to bank daylight for the six-hour exit. Add 1-2 hours if FR 38 is gated and you are walking or biking road miles.

row.detailed_rack: Light alpine kit rather than a rock rack. One 60 m rope is enough for the documented rappels (Abegg's party carried two 60 m ropes and used them for a single double-rope rappel from near the top, and noted one rope would have sufficed at the col). Bring 2-3 ice screws for the 50-degree ice, a picket or two for snow anchors, a small selection of nuts and slings for rock anchors on the fourth-class band and summit mixed ground, and a generous amount of cord/webbing plus rap rings — there are no reliable fixed anchors and you should plan to leave gear. One technical ice tool plus a mountaineering axe is a reasonable compromise for AI1 mixed ground; Abegg's party used single axes.
what_to_bring: Snowshoes or approach skis for the lower Green Creek basin
Headlamp plus spare batteries (the documented exit was after dark)
Sturdy boots and dry socks for the unbridged Middle Fork Nooksack log crossing
GPS or phone with the track preloaded offline
Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass for the trailhead
Small first aid and repair kit
Bike, if FR 38 is gated at Wallace Creek
pro_tips: Scout the Middle Fork Nooksack log crossing before you commit to the day — its location moves. One party used a log about 200 yards east of the trail junction, another an unofficial log a quarter mile downstream of the usual crossing.
The Green Creek climbers' path leaves the Elbow Lake Trail just before a sharp switchback near Hildebrand Creek and is marked with small blue diamonds; missing it costs hours.

Check the Forest Service Mt Baker-Snoqualmie alerts page before you drive — FR 38 was closed at milepost 7 for a washout as of a 27 July 2026 alert, which blocks vehicle access to the Elbow Lake Trailhead entirely.
Snowshoes can be left at the snow line and picked up on the way down; the upper basin is firm enough for crampons alone in a good spring freeze.
A single 60 m rope covers the documented rappels, so there is no need to haul two unless you want a double-rope rappel from high on the line.

The 6,240+ ft col southeast of the summit is the natural gear-up and decision point. Steep snow just below it was reported unpleasant to downclimb, so plan to rappel it rather than discovering that at dusk.
This is the shortest technical objective on the peak — if the weather cooperates, it links naturally with Cinderella Peak just across the col.
watch_out: Steep 50-degree ice/mixed terrain with two rappels on the descent, one from near the top and one below the col.
row.pro_needs: Protection is thin and improvised. The 50-degree ice takes screws when it is real ice and takes nothing when it is unconsolidated snow over rock, which is the more common case. The fourth-class rock band and the mixed summit ground offer occasional horns, blocks and small nut placements in the dunite, which is coarse and generally solid but is not a splitter-crack medium. Plan on running it out on moderate snow and saving your gear for anchors. Because you will rappel the line, budget cord and rings for two stations you may have to build from scratch.
row.best_season: Documented ascent/descent was mid-May in a ski-mountaineering context (spring snowpack); this is not established as a summer rock route.
row.approach: From the Elbow Lake Trailhead on Forest Road 38 (Middle Fork Nooksack Road), the Elbow Lake Trail reaches the Middle Fork Nooksack River within a few minutes. THE BRIDGE IS GONE and has been for decades — the Forest Service states plainly that there is no bridge over the river to reach the north trailhead and that fording may not be possible during high flows. Parties cross on whatever log is currently in place. One group used a log crossing roughly 200 yards east of the trail junction; another used an unofficial log about a quarter mile downstream of the usual crossing. Assume you will have to hunt for it, and treat the crossing as the crux of the day in terms of consequence. Once across, follow the Elbow Lake Trail — reported in remarkably good shape — through old-growth for about 1.5 miles. Just before a sharp switchback (near Hildebrand Creek), find the blazed Green Creek climbers' path branching off and heading up the Green Creek drainage. It is marked with small blue diamond trail markers. Follow it past the Wiseman Lake outlet at about 2,850 ft, then up through the brush-filled Green Creek valley, past a rock buttress around 3,800 ft, and onto loose scree, boulder fields and rolling slabs with class 3 scrambling to gain the Green Creek Glacier. The Green Glacier approach is 5 miles one way with 4,000 ft of gain from the trailhead over trail, climbers' trail, boulder fields, scree and slabs. For the South Couloir specifically, continue up the basin and climb snow to the 6,240+ ft col southeast of Little Sister, then traverse onto the south side and up into the gully. In deep winter one party found hard snow all the way to the col; snowshoes were left at the snow line and crampons carried from there.
row.descent_text: Reverse the line: one winter party made a double-rope rappel from near the top and a second rappel below the col southeast of the summit, where a single 60 m rope reaches. The couloir has also been skied.
row.bail: The line is short enough to retreat from at almost any point with two rappels or one 60 m rappel plus downclimbing, so the real bail decisions happen lower. Turn around at the Middle Fork Nooksack if the log crossing looks marginal — high flows on the Middle Fork have no safe alternative and the Forest Service warns fording may not be possible. If avalanche conditions in the Green Creek basin look wrong, the basin itself is the hazard, not the couloir, and there is no alternative line of ascent. From the 6,240+ ft col, walking away costs you nothing but the summit. Once in the gully, bail is straightforward: build a rock anchor, rappel to the col, and descend south-side snow.

pitch_detail.notes: About 40 m of fourth-class rock forms the entry to the line, per the published description of the Twin Sister High Route. On the ski descent this section was protected and rappelled. Depending on snow year this can be buried, in which case it climbs as moderate snow.

First rope length of the 100+ m of 50-degree ice and mixed rock described in the published account. A winter party climbed this ground unroped in firm conditions, describing it as a snow-and-rock slope/gully. Screws where there is real ice; often only snow over rock.

Second rope length, finishing with a bit of mixed climbing on reasonably solid rock near the summit; third-class scrambling on the final sections. The 100+ m section is split here into two rope lengths for planning — it is a continuous 100+ m, not discrete pitches.

row.itinerary: Part of a 3-day, ~26-mile south-to-north ski traverse of the whole range (Step Sister, Last Sister, Saddle Slab, Nancy, Barbara, Trisolace, Cinderella, Little Sister, Hayden, Skookum, South Twin, North Twin, and an unnamed peak called Mirage), with roughly 12,000 ft gained and 14,000 ft lost overall — not just on Little Sister.

climate.fall: Generally out of condition — old snow gone, new snow not yet consolidated, and the Green Creek approach back to brush and boulders. Not a recommended window for this line.
climate.spring: The prime window for this route. April-May typically offers a consolidated snowpack in the couloir, snow cover over the brushy lower Green Creek approach, and lengthening daylight — but the FR 38 gate at Wallace Creek is generally still closed, so expect extra road miles on foot or bike. Wet-slab and loose-wet avalanche problems develop on south aspects as the day warms.
climate.summer: The couloir goes out of condition. Snow retreats, moats open, and the south side becomes loose rock. Summer is rock-route season on this peak; see the West Face, North Face and Southeast Ridge.
climate.winter: Climbable but serious. One party did it on 31 January 2015 in hard-snow conditions and suspected it was a first winter ascent. Short days force a dark exit, the unbridged river crossing is at its most unpleasant, and the Green Creek basin carries a full avalanche problem. Consult the NWAC West Slopes North forecast.
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate with very high winter precipitation. Most weather systems arrive off the Pacific and hit the Twin Sisters before Mount Baker, so the range takes the brunt of incoming fronts. Drainage is into the Middle Fork Nooksack via Green, Sister, Skookum and Howard creeks.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC West Slopes North (Mt Baker area). NWAC issues daily avalanche and mountain weather forecasts from roughly mid-November through mid-April.

approach_variants.name: Green Creek Glacier to the 6,240+ ft col southeast of the summit, then round onto the south side
approach_variants.notes:
From the Elbow Lake Trailhead on Forest Road 38, Elbow Lake Trail #697 reaches the Middle Fork Nooksack within a few minutes. THE BRIDGE IS GONE and has been for decades — the Forest Service states plainly that there is no bridge to the north trailhead and that fording may not be possible at high flows. Parties cross on whatever log is currently there: one recorded party used a log roughly 200 yards east of the trail junction, another an unofficial log about a quarter mile downstream of the usual crossing. Assume you will have to hunt for it and treat the crossing as the most consequential thing you do all day.

Once across, follow Elbow Lake Trail — reported in remarkably good shape — through old growth for about 1.5 miles. Just before a sharp switchback near Hildebrand Creek, find the blazed Green Creek climbers' path branching off up the Green Creek drainage, marked with small blue diamonds.

Follow it past the Wiseman Lake outlet at about 2,850 ft, up through the brush-filled valley, past a rock buttress around 3,800 ft, and onto loose scree, boulder fields and rolling slabs with Class 3 scrambling to gain the Green Creek Glacier. That is roughly five miles one way and 4,000 ft of gain from the trailhead.

In deep winter, snowshoes have been left at the snow line and crampons carried from there.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jan-May. This is a snow line and a winter ascent of it is on record; in deep winter parties have found hard snow all the way to the col
hazards: A bridgeless Middle Fork Nooksack crossing that must be hunted for and is the day's biggest consequence
A south-facing snow gully — timing matters and it warms
A line with no recorded climbing first ascent and very little traffic
Two rappels on the descent, one from near the top and one below the col
Loose scree, boulder fields and Class 3 slabs to reach the glacier
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE COL SOUTHEAST OF THE SUMMIT, AT 6,240 FT OR A LITTLE ABOVE, IS THE HINGE OF THE WHOLE ROUTE — AND THE COULOIR IS ON THE FAR SIDE OF IT. From the basin, climb snow to that col. Then TRAVERSE ONTO THE SOUTH SIDE and up into the gully. Nothing on the Green Creek side of the col is this route; you have to go over.

SO THE TEST IS AN ASPECT FLIP, WHICH IS THE MOST RELIABLE KIND IN CLOUD. You approach on the NORTH-facing Green Creek side, in shade, on the glacier. You climb on the SOUTH side, out of the basin you walked in through. If you are still looking at the glacier you came up, you have not crossed the col.

CONFIRM THE COL BY ITS NUMBER AND ITS POSITION: 6,240+ ft, and SOUTHEAST of the summit. It is the col between Little Sister and Cinderella, the same one the Southeast Ridge starts from.

WINTER CHANGES WHERE THE APPROACH ENDS, NOT WHERE THE ROUTE STARTS. In deep winter, hard snow has run continuously to the col, which makes the walk simpler and the col no less the marker.

BE CLEAR ABOUT THE RECORD ON THIS LINE, because it affects what you should expect to find: no rock or ice first ascent is recorded. What is documented is a ski descent of the line during a traverse of the range, and a party in January 2015 reporting a suspected first winter ascent of the peak by this south-side ground. The winter party came down it with two rappels, one from near the top and one below the col. That is not a well-trodden route with a bootpack in it.

name: Southeast Route
prior_findings: No source names a 'Southeast Route' or gives it Grade IV 5.8; the 1961 first ascent was class 4 via a ledge onto the north face; notes now say it faces NW. Identity review.

earlier_research.evidence: This row's overview (2015) is correct per the AAJ report, Alpinist and the FA trip report (July 6, 2015); the sister Stonehenge row was wrong and is fixed in its own result.

The 1961 first-ascent account (AAJ 1962) describes a class IV line following a ledge onto the north face from the west notch; Wikipedia lists the easiest route only as class 5, and the row's own corrections note cites an 'awkward 5.7 step-around'. No source names a 'Southeast Route' or gives Grade IV 5.8, but a replacement grade (and the commitment/alpine grade to match) is not settled by two sources.

earlier_research.evidence: The FA account climbs from the west (Himmel-Otto) notch via a ledge onto the north face, supporting the NW fields; but no source describes a route called 'Southeast Route', so it is unclear whether the row's name or its prose is the error. One source only; left open.

The published Crescent Creek approach and the FA account mention no glacier on the route, but the lower Barrier crossing runs at the toe of the Terror Glacier, and no source states whether parties rope up for glacier travel. Not settled by two sources.

No external source gives a rappel count or a false-summit-notch descent for this line (that false-summit notch belongs to Wild Hair Crack's description). The descent is undocumented beyond reversing the route.

The summit pin matches the peak's published coordinate (48.77639, -121.31472); the camp/gully pins sit well south, so the defect is pin placement, which is out of scope. The distMi values are unsourced but in order, so they are not nulled.

The 1961 first-ascent account describes a class IV line from the west notch via a ledge onto the north face; Wikipedia gives the normal route only as YDS class 5 (5.7 in an earlier revision); the current Himmelhorn area page describes the standard way as a snow/scree gully to the Himmel-Otto col with a class 3/4 bypass near the top. No source gives Grade IV 5.8, but the sources disagree between class 4 and low/mid 5th, so no replacement grade (with matching commitment/alpine grade) is settled. Would settle: the Himmelhorn entry in the Beckey Cascade Alpine Guide vol. 3, or a trip report of the standard route stating its grade.

On the row, aspect, face, approach, climbing_route label and the approach_variants note all say northwest; only the climbing_route note, the day-2 itinerary note and its copy in the timing breakdown say southeast. The route NAME is out of scope and left as is.

earlier_research.evidence: The Himmelhorn area page describes the whole way as the Stump Hollow approach, a crossing into Crescent Creek Basin and a narrow snow/scree gully to the Himmel-Otto col, with no glacier. An independent 2023 trip report over the same Goodell Creek - Stump Hollow - Barrier approach to the Crescent Creek camp below Terror mentions snow patches but no glacier crossing or roped glacier travel. A Picket Range approach page describes the Barrier crossings as ledge/moat crossings at the ends of the Terror Glacier, not across it. So the crevasse panel is right and the rope note / descent text glacier mentions are removed.

No new source states a season window for this route; the only dated record is an October 4, 2020 ascent from the same col (Wild Hair Crack), which supports October against the four internal fields ending in September. The row's own itinerary and timing already say one day each way; partner requirements, a hazard line and the turnaround text still said the approach itself was multi-day.

The Crescent Creek Basin Camp waypoint and the bivy entry give 6,050 ft, while the same waypoint's directions and itinerary day 1 say about 5,800 ft. One trip report camped at a 6,400 ft bench (Chopping Block camp) and the basin has camps at several heights, so no single figure is settled by two sources; a topo reading of the specific bench this route uses would settle it.

row.name: Southeast Route
row.fa: Ed Cooper, Glen Denny, Joan Firey, Joe Firey, George Whitmore — September 8, 1961 (also the peak's overall first ascent)
gear: crampons (early season, for the approach gully and Barrier crossing)
hazards: sustained exposure
loose/chossy rock on the upper peak and approach gully
remoteness — a full-day approach each way with no quick escape
The Barrier crossing between Terror and Crescent Creek basins: steep, loose, exposed traverse
route-finding through brush and cliff bands on the Goodell Creek approach
lingering moats and icy snow in the Himmel-Otto col gully in early/late season
row.overview: Himmelhorn (originally Himmelgeisterhorn, "Horn of the Sky Spirit") is one of the most sought-after summits of the Southern Pickets, sitting on the crest between Ottohorn/Frenzel Spitz to the west and Twin Needles/Mount Terror to the east, with the small Mustard Glacier draped on its north side. It was first climbed September 8, 1961 by Ed Cooper, Glen Denny, Joan Firey, Joe Firey, and George Whitmore, who approached via the west notch (the Himmel-Otto col) and found a class 4 line up a ledge system onto the north/northwest face — no summit cairn was found, confirming the true first ascent. The peak remains a serious objective less for sustained technical difficulty than for its position deep in one of the most remote, brush-choked corners of North Cascades National Park; parties commonly link it with neighboring Ottohorn and/or Frenzel Spitz from a shared Crescent Creek Basin camp. Other established lines on the peak include the classic Wild Hair Crack (5.7, west face, Kroeker/Roper/Wild, 1981) and the harder South Face "Stonehenge" (5.10-, 8 pitches, Schilling/Halder, 2015).
row.beta: First ascensionists Cooper, Denny, and the Fireys found the peak unpromising from either flanking notch, then located a class-4 route by following a ledge onto the north face that wasn't visible from below. The line is mostly scrambling with short steeper steps; conditions and difficulty vary considerably with season and snow coverage in the approach gully.
row.turnaround: Given the full-day approach and lack of any fast escape, set a firm summit-day turnaround time and factor in the extra hours needed to get back to the col and basin camp before dark.
row.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
row.comms: Cell service is unreliable throughout this part of North Cascades National Park; the park explicitly warns not to rely on cell phones for emergency plans in this terrain, though occasional signal may be caught from high points.

waypoints.name: Goodell Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Old roadbed starts at the Goodell Creek group campground turnout off SR 20 (milepost 119) near Newhalem; NPS wilderness permit required for overnight; no parking pass is needed at this National Park trailhead.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR 20 about 60 miles - roughly an hour and a half - east from Burlington and park at the Goodell Creek Campground turnout at milepost 119, just west of Newhalem. The highway is paved all the way to here, and the trailhead sits west of both of SR 20's winter closure gates (Ross Dam at milepost 134, and Newhalem at milepost 120 in harder winters), so driving access to this trailhead does not depend on the seasonal opening of the highway east of the park.

waypoints.name: Roadbed End / Basin Fork
waypoints.note: The 4-mile old roadbed peters out at a stone cairn in a wide clearing; the defined path forks right toward Terror Creek Basin, while a fainter boot path continues straight for the Crescent Creek Basin / Stump Hollow approach used for Himmelhorn, Ottohorn, and Frenzel Spitz.
waypoints.directions: Follow the old decommissioned logging roadbed upstream along the true left (south) side of Goodell Creek. It is grassy and gravelly, flat and easy walking for roughly 4 to 4.5 miles, gaining only a few hundred feet from the ~600 ft trailhead to about 1,700-1,800 ft. The end of it is not obvious from the tread - watch on the right, in the wide clearing, for the cairn or stone marker climbers call the 'stone arrow', which is what marks the unsigned climbers' path leaving the creek bottom.

waypoints.name: Treeline Breakout
waypoints.note: Boot path breaks out of old-growth forest onto steep heather benches and slab; the steep, brushy tread above the roadbed is easy to lose in fog.
waypoints.directions: Top off water at Goodell Creek before leaving the roadbed: there is none reliable again until treeline. From the cairn, the boot path leaves the creek bottom and switchbacks steeply up into old-growth forest toward Stump Hollow. Expect steep root-and-duff footing with slide alder and devil's club low down; the path stays reasonably distinct with flagging and cairns higher up, but multiple trip reports on this approach describe losing it, and it is especially easy to lose in fog - track it deliberately rather than trusting the tread to hold. Around 5,000-5,600 ft the timber gives way to the heather benches and slab of Stump Hollow, a slabby basin wedged between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block.

waypoints.name: Terror-Crescent Divide Saddle
waypoints.note: Rising traverse gains this ~6,200 ft saddle on the ridge dividing Terror Creek and Crescent Creek basins; drop west off the saddle into Crescent Creek Basin from here.
waypoints.directions: From Stump Hollow, make a rising traverse over meadow, slab and - early to mid season - snow to the broad saddle at roughly 6,200 ft on the Barrier, the ridge dividing Terror Creek basin from Crescent Creek basin. Carry an ice axe for this, and crampons early season.

waypoints.name: Crescent Creek Basin Streams
waypoints.note: Two snowmelt streams run off the slabs above camp; reliable early-to-mid season but reported to thin out by late August in dry years.
waypoints.directions: This leg is the Barrier crossing, the most exposed piece of the approach and one of the route's named hazards. Cross by one of two options: a lower line on a loose, exposed ledge system at the toe of the Terror Glacier, or a higher line over moat terrain and steep choss just below Mt. Degenhardt. Either takes under an hour, but both are loose enough that rockfall onto anyone below is the real hazard - helmets on, and do not stack the party. Drop the far (west) side of the saddle into Crescent Creek Basin, where two snowmelt streams run off the slabs; they are reliable early to mid season but reported to thin out by late August in dry years, so plan your water around that rather than assuming they run.

waypoints.name: Crescent Creek Basin Camp
waypoints.note: Established gravel-and-heather camp on slabs used as the base for Himmelhorn, Ottohorn, and Frenzel Spitz; reach it via the stump-hollow traverse rather than the Terror Basin path.
waypoints.directions: A last short step across the gravel and heather slabs from the stream draws to the established basin camp at roughly 5,800 ft below Mt. Terror. This is the standard base for Himmelhorn, Ottohorn and Frenzel Spitz, and it is reached by the Stump Hollow traverse rather than by the Terror Basin path. Camping here is at-large with no designated sites, but an NPS backcountry permit is required for the overnight, and a park-wide moratorium bans new fixed anchors - plan on clean, removable gear for everything above.

waypoints.name: Himmel-Otto Col Gully
waypoints.note: Narrow gully gains the Himmel-Otto col between Himmelhorn and Ottohorn; straightforward snow early season, but by late season expect icy neve, chossy moats, and an overhanging boulder near the top forcing a loose class 3/4 bypass on climber's left.
waypoints.directions: From camp, climb the narrow gully leading to the Himmel-Otto col between Himmelhorn and Ottohorn. What this leg actually is depends entirely on season. Early, it is a straightforward snow climb with a bit of scrambling near the top: axe, and crampons if it has firmed up. Late, the same gully is icy hardpack with choss-filled moats along the rock margins, and an overhanging boulder near the col commonly forces a loose, exposed Class 3-4 bypass on the climber's left. Coming back down late season, parties often find fixed or placed rappel anchors in the moat sections more trustworthy than downclimbing loose rock alongside hard snow - there are no bolted stations anywhere on this route, so carry slings, cord and tat to build your own.

waypoints.name: Himmelhorn Summit
waypoints.note: True summit (7,880 ft); the Southeast Route finishes via crack systems on the face above the col — downclimb and rappel the same line back to the Himmel-Otto col to descend.

sectionBreakdown.note: From the Goodell Creek trailhead, follow an old roadbed about 4-4.5 miles, then leave the maintained trail to climb the brushy forested ridge crest, cross Terror Creek on a log jam…
An alpine-start day climb from Crescent Creek Basin: ascend the narrow snow/scree gully to the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col, then work up the northwest side to the summit, downclimbing …

row.detailed_rack: A light alpine rack is typical for this class-IV/low-5th line: a small set of nuts and cams, a few slings/draws, and a lightweight rope for the short technical sections and any rappels off the col; carry an ice axe and crampons for the approach gully and col when snow-covered (common through mid-summer).
what_to_bring: Ice axe (and crampons in early season) for the approach gully and Barrier crossing
Overnight/bivy gear for the Crescent Creek Basin camp
pro_tips: Time the trip for a stable high-pressure window in Aug–early Sept; the range sees little traffic and a rescue is a day-plus out.
Carry a satellite communicator (inReach/SPOT) — there is no cell coverage in the Pickets.
File a wilderness/climbing itinerary at the Marblemount WIC even on a day the permit isn't strictly required, so rangers know your plan.
Early-season parties should carry an ice axe (and consider crampons) for the Himmel-Otto col gully; by late season the same gully turns to loose scree and chossy moats.

Call the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center for current route/approach and gully/moat conditions before heading in — trip reports for this peak are sparse and conditions vary significantly year to year.
watch_out: The Barrier crossing (~6,100 ft) between Terror and Crescent Creek basins — steep, loose, exposed grass/rock traverse
Loose, chossy rock high on the peak and in the approach gully
Slide-alder and cliff-band bushwhacking if descending directly via Goodell Creek
Lingering moats and icy snow in the col gully in early or late season
row.pro_needs: Protection needs are modest and intermittent — mostly natural gear placements on broken, blocky rock for short exposed sections rather than sustained crack climbing.
row.best_season: Late July through early September gives the most reliable snow-free rock and safest approach-gully conditions; snow and moats can linger into July, and early-fall storms often close the window by mid-September.
row.approach: From the Goodell Creek Campground/Trailhead on SR 20 just west of Newhalem (~600 ft), follow the old decommissioned logging roadbed along the true left (south) side of Goodell Creek. This grassy/gravel roadbed is flat and easy hiking for roughly 4 to 4.5 miles, gaining only a few hundred feet to about 1,700-1,800 ft. Watch on the right for a cairn/stone marker (climbers call it the 'stone arrow') at the end of the roadbed - this marks the unsigned but well-boot-beaten climbers' path that leaves the creek bottom and switchbacks steeply up into old-growth forest toward Stump Hollow and Terror Creek Basin. This user trail is steep, root-and-duff footing, and brushy in spots (slide alder, devil's club low down) but stays reasonably distinct with flagging/cairns in the upper sections; there is no reliable water between the roadbed's end and treeline, so top off at Goodell Creek. Around 5,000-5,600 ft the forest opens into Stump Hollow, a slabby heather-and-snowfield basin wedged between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block - a scenic, easier-angle respite after the timber grind. From Stump Hollow, rising-traverse on meadow, slab, and (early/mid-season) snow to a broad saddle on the Barrier ridge at roughly 6,200 ft. Cross the Barrier itself by one of two options: a lower crossing on a loose, exposed ledge system at the toe of the Terror Glacier, or a higher crossing over moat terrain and steep choss just below Mt. Degenhardt; either takes under an hour but involves loose rock and some exposure, so care with rockfall onto any party below is essential. Descend the far side into Crescent Creek Basin (good bivy sites and reliable running water, roughly below Mt. Terror) - this is the standard camp for Himmelhorn objectives. From camp, ascend the narrow gully leading to the Himmel-Otto col: in early season this is a straightforward snow climb with a bit of scrambling near the top; by late season the gully turns to icy hardpack with choss-filled moats along the rock margins, and an overhanging boulder near the col often forces a loose, exposed class 3-4 bypass on the left (climber's) side. From the col, the standard route continues up easier ground (scrambling to low 5th class) onto Himmelhorn's northwest flank to the 7,880 ft summit. Total approach distance to the summit and back runs on the order of 15-16 miles round trip with substantial elevation gain and loss, so most parties treat this as a 2-4 day trip with a basecamp in Crescent Creek Basin rather than a car-to-car push.
row.descent_text: Descend by reversing the route: downclimb (with short rappels where the rock steepens or is wet/icy) from the summit back down to the Himmel-Otto col, then retrace the approach gully back down into Crescent Creek Basin. Early in the season this gully descent is a quick, straightforward snow glissade/plunge-step with minimal fuss; by late season, when the gully has melted out to icy hardpack and choss-filled moats, parties often find fixed or placed rap anchors in the moat sections more reliable than downclimbing loose rock next to hard snow/ice. From Crescent Creek Basin, reverse the entire approach: recross the Barrier (lower ledge or upper moat/choss option), drop back through Stump Hollow, and pick up the steep climbers' path back down through the timber to the old Goodell Creek roadbed and out to the trailhead. There are no bolted or fixed rappel stations on this route - any anchors encountered or built (slings around horns/blocks/chockstones) are natural, climber-placed gear anchors typical of this remote, seldom-visited range, so carry a small rack of slings/cord and a couple of rappel-rated tat-worthy items in case the moat or upper gully requires a rappel to protect the loose, exposed terrain near the col. A single 60m rope is adequate for any rappels on this route (the terrain near the col is broken into short steps, not a sustained wall). Watch for rockfall in the gully and on the Barrier crossings, especially with parties above, and for the choss/loose-rock hazard around the overhanging boulder bypass near the col, which is exposed in both directions.
row.bail: Retreat from high on the route is by reversing rappels/downclimbing back to the Himmel-Otto col — there is no quicker way down. From the col, the approach gully is the only reasonable descent to Crescent Creek Basin.

itinerary.cal: North Cascades NP backcountry permit required for the Crescent Creek/Terror Basin camp; route is typically in reasonable condition July-September once the approach brush and access road are snow-free.

days.note: From the Goodell Creek trailhead, follow an old roadbed about 4-4.5 miles, then leave the maintained trail to climb the brushy forested ridge crest, cross Terror Creek on a log jam, and continue through Stump Hollow into Crescent Creek Basin. It's a steep, brushy, unmaintained climbers' path with route-finding required; camp on heather/slabs around 5,800 ft below Terror and Himmelhorn.
days.title: Approach to Crescent Creek Basin

days.note: An alpine-start day climb from Crescent Creek Basin: ascend the narrow snow/scree gully to the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col, then work up the northwest side to the summit, downclimbing or bypassing an overhanging block near the top on class 3/4 rock in late season. Descend by reversing the route, downclimbing and rappelling the gully back to camp.
