access.fees: $10 per person backcountry camping fee plus a $6 nonrefundable reservation fee, charged mid-May through early October (fee structure updated March 2024); no charge mid-October through mid-May.
access.notes: 60% of sites are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Designated wilderness — a park-wide moratorium bans new fixed anchors; use clean, removable protection. Camping in the Southern Pickets is at-large (no designated sites) but still subject to permit/quota rules.
access.permit: A backcountry/wilderness permit is required for all overnight stays in Terror Basin or Crescent Creek Basin, obtained in person (walk-up) or via advance reservation at the North Cascades NP Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount (360-854-7245); no separate permit is needed for the climb itself, only for overnight camping.
access.closures: SR 20 (North Cascades Highway) closes seasonally east of Newhalem — typically early December to mid/late April — starting at the Ross Dam Trailhead gate (MP 134) and, as conditions worsen later in winter, moving down to the Newhalem gate (MP 120), out to the Silver Star gate (MP 171) due to avalanche hazard; the Goodell Creek Trailhead at MP 119 sits west of both gates and is reachable year-round from the Marblemount/Newhalem side; the route itself is only realistically climbable July–September.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park (National Park Service)
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)

overnight_permit.what: North Cascades NP backcountry permit for the cross-country zone, with a fee
overnight_permit.where: Reserve on Recreation.gov, then get the permit by email or in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; walk-up permits are issued there the day of or the day before.

road.name: State Route 20 (North Cascades Highway) to Goodell Creek Trailhead/Campground, MP 119, near Newhalem
road.status: Paved and open year-round to this point — it sits just west of the winter closure gates at Ross Dam Trailhead (MP 134) and, later in winter, Newhalem (MP 120)
road.driveNote: About 60 miles / 1.5 hrs east of Burlington via SR 20; park at Goodell Creek Campground.
road.seasonalGate: SR 20 itself closes seasonally further east (roughly early Dec–mid/late April), starting at the Ross Dam Trailhead gate (MP 134) and moving down to the Newhalem gate (MP 120) in harsher conditions, out to Silver Star (MP 171) — but this does not affect access to Goodell Creek (MP 119), which sits west of both gates.

climate.typical: Marine west-coast climate typical of the North Cascades crest: frequent Pacific frontal precipitation (heaviest Nov–Mar) with a wet, dense snowpack; the Pickets hold snow late into the season on north-facing terrain, and approach gullies can remain snow-filled into July. Even in a good summer week, expect the possibility of afternoon cloud buildup and fast-moving weather off the Pacific.
climate.forecastZone: No NWAC avalanche forecast covers this zone in summer; use an NWS point forecast for the Mount Terror/Picket Range area (forecast.weather.gov) for current conditions.

emergency.notes: This is one of the most remote objectives in the Lower 48 — carry a satellite communicator (inReach/SPOT), as there is no cell coverage, and expect NPS response times to the Southern Pickets to be a day or more.
emergency.rangerStation: North Cascades National Park Wilderness Information Center, 7280 Ranger Station Rd, Marblemount, WA — 360-854-7245 (permits, current trail/route conditions, and backcountry emergency coordination).
emergency.nearestHospital: PeaceHealth United General Medical Center, 2000 Hospital Dr, Sedro-Woolley, WA (24-hour ER) — roughly 60 miles / ~1.5 hr drive from the Goodell Creek trailhead via SR 20.
emergency.sheriffDispatch: 911, routed to North Cascades NP dispatch; technical mountain rescue in the Picket Range is typically coordinated by NPS climbing rangers with mutual aid from Whatcom County Search & Rescue (Bellingham Mountain Rescue unit).

crowds.peakTraffic: if any, a handful of parties in late July-August during the short dry-rock window; often zero attempts in a given week
crowds.estimatePerSeason: roughly 5-15 parties per season - among the least-visited technical objectives in the Cascades

fitnessSpec.hiking: Strong off-trail/bushwhack fitness for a long, full-day approach (Goodell Creek/Stump Hollow into Crescent Creek basin) with sustained elevation gain on unmaintained terrain
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Heavy multi-day pack (camp gear, food, rock rack) for at least a 3-4 day trip

partner_requirements.approachTime: A full, long approach day each way from Goodell Creek trailhead via Stump Hollow into Crescent Creek basin before the climb itself
requiredSkills: 5.8 alpine rock climbing on unfamiliar, loose gneiss
Route-finding among gendarmes with minimal beta/marked path
Self-rescue and remote wilderness first aid (no quick evac)
Backcountry camping and Leave No Trace practice in a NPS wilderness zone
Multi-pitch anchor building and rappelling on exposed terrain
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Advanced alpine climber with prior grade III-IV alpine rock experience; comfortable route-finding through unmarked gendarme terrain far from rescue

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through early September; narrows further to late July-August for most reliably dry rock

July.reason: Early July can still hold lingering snow/moats on approach and route ('snowbound' in spring bleeding into early summer); conditions improve to good by mid-to-late July

August.reason: Most reliable dry rock and stable weather window ('best season for dry rock')

September.reason: Early September typically still stable and dry; late September risk increases as fall storms arrive

weather.typical: Remote alpine climate requiring a stable high-pressure window; conditions shift quickly and remoteness raises the cost of getting caught out
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorm buildup is possible on unstable summer days in the North Cascades, as on nearby Pickets objectives; no route-specific storm-frequency data found

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Sustained exposure on steep gneiss with route-finding through gendarmes to a small, exposed summit; loose rock adds fall/rockfall consequence, and the deep remoteness of the Southern Pickets means any fall or injury involves a multi-day self-extraction or major rescue effort

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer rock route; falls outside NWAC's operational forecast season (roughly Nov-May) and no Pickets-specific zone exists

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: N/A - no significant glacier travel on this route; the Crescent Creek basin approach may cross residual seasonal snowfields, especially earlier in the window

gaps: The exact modern technical grade of the original 1961 line is disputed in available sources — the first-ascent account calls it a Class 4 route, while the on-file "Grade IV, 5.8" figure could not be independently confirmed against a primary topo, so it was left as-is rather than guessed at.

No confirmed pitch count, detailed rack, or GPS/mileage waypoints exist in available sources specifically for this line (as opposed to the separately-documented Wild Hair Crack and Stonehenge routes).

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek and the stone arrow, Stump Hollow, the Barrier, and the Himmel-Otto col gully
approach_variants.notes: From the Goodell Creek Campground and trailhead on SR-20 just west of Newhalem at about 600 ft, follow the old decommissioned logging roadbed along the south side of Goodell Creek. It is flat and easy for roughly 4-4.5 miles, gaining only a few hundred feet to about 1,700-1,800 ft. Watch on the right for a cairn and stone marker, which climbers call the stone arrow, at the end of the roadbed. This marks the unsigned but well-boot-beaten climbers' path that leaves the creek bottom and switchbacks steeply into old-growth forest toward Stump Hollow and Terror Creek Basin. Steep, root-and-duff footing, brushy in spots, but reasonably distinct with flagging and cairns higher. No reliable water between the roadbed's end and treeline, so top off at Goodell Creek. Around 5,000-5,600 ft the forest opens into Stump Hollow, a slabby heather-and-snowfield basin wedged between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block. From there, rising-traverse on meadow, slab and early-season snow to a broad saddle on the Barrier ridge at roughly 6,200 ft, then cross the Barrier into Crescent Creek Basin, the standard camp for Himmelhorn objectives. NOTE ON THE NAME: this route is titled Southeast Route, but the published standard route on this peak is on the NORTHWEST aspect, and its aspect is already recorded as NW.
hazards: An icy, choss-and-moat gully to the col in late season
An overhanging boulder near the col forcing a loose, exposed class 3-4 bypass
Two Barrier crossings, both loose and exposed, with rockfall onto any party below
No reliable water between the Goodell roadbed and treeline
No bolted or fixed rappel stations anywhere on the route; all anchors are built
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE STARTS AT A COL YOU REACH BY A NARROW GULLY, AND THE GULLY'S CHARACTER CHANGES COMPLETELY THROUGH THE SEASON. From the Crescent Creek Basin camp, ascend the narrow gully leading to the HIMMEL-OTTO COL. In early season that is a straightforward snow climb with a bit of scrambling near the top. By late season it turns to icy hardpack with choss-filled moats along the rock margins, and AN OVERHANGING BOULDER NEAR THE COL OFTEN FORCES A LOOSE, EXPOSED CLASS 3-4 BYPASS ON THE LEFT, climber's left.

SO THE MARKER IS THE BOULDER, AND IT IS A COUNTABLE ONE: there is one overhanging boulder near the top of the gully, and getting past it on its left is the last obstacle before the col. If you have bypassed several such blocks, you are in the wrong gully.

ARRIVAL: you are at the col when the gully tops out into a gap with ground falling away on the far side. From there the standard route continues on easier ground, scrambling to low 5th class, onto Himmelhorn's northwest flank to the 7,880 ft summit.

TWO CROSSINGS OF THE BARRIER EXIST AND BOTH ARE CORRECT: a LOWER crossing on a loose, exposed ledge system at the toe of the Terror Glacier, or a HIGHER crossing over moat terrain and steep choss just below Mount Degenhardt. Either takes under an hour. Both are loose enough that a party above another is the real danger.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: descending north from the Himmel-Otto col rather than climbing from it. The north side is a different and harder proposition and leads onto the Mustard Glacier.

climbing_route.label: Northwest flank from the Himmel-Otto col
climbing_route.notes: From the col the Southeast Route continues up easier ground on Himmelhorn's northwest flank to the 7,880 ft summit.

bivy.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: Crescent Creek Basin sits on the north side of the crest and is what you cross the Barrier for, reached over the roughly 6,400 ft saddle northeast of the Chopping Block. It is the working base for East and West McMillan Spire, Inspiration, the Twin Needles, and for the Ottohorn and Himmelhorn by way of the col between them; Frenzel Spitz sits off the main chain near the Ottohorn's north side. Parties camp at several benches at different heights.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and pools fed by the basin's snowfields, reliable early and mid season and unreliable late once the snow has pulled back. Plan on melting snow in a lean year.
bivy.permit: This is the SEPARATE Crescent Creek cross-country zone, not Terror Basin — a trip camping in both needs both zones written onto the same permit, night by night. Like Terror Basin it is walk-up only at Marblemount rather than bookable in advance.
bivy.capacity: A few parties on gravel, slab and snow; the zone is capped at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
bivy.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
bivy.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
bivy.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
bivy.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

bivy.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
bivy.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
bivy.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is LEGALLY AWKWARD: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
bivy.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
bivy.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is NOT on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is WALK-UP ONLY — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Stump Hollow bench
bivy.notes: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only. Trickles and small pools are dependable through early summer while snow lingers, and can dry up or retreat entirely by late season; late-summer parties should expect to search or carry.
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone permit from the Wilderness Information Center. This bench sits close to the divide between the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones, so ask which zone the rangers are writing you into rather than assuming — the answer decides what the rest of your itinerary can say.
bivy.capacity: Small — a couple of parties on heather benches and slabs, and it is easy to end up spread out

bivy.name: High bivouacs at the western end of the crest
bivy.notes: The western summits — the Twin Needles, Ottohorn, Himmelhorn and Frenzel Spitz — are far enough along the crest that a party working from a basin camp faces a very long day, so some take a bivouac high on the traverse instead. These are improvised spots rather than established sites, and quality varies from a decent gravel bench to a night sitting on a ledge. There is no shelter and no water, so this only makes sense with a settled forecast and a party willing to move fast the next morning.
bivy.water: No dependable source. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs: carry water up or melt snow, and expect nothing at all once the summer snow has gone.
bivy.permit: Still inside a cross-country zone and still requires a wilderness permit with the night assigned to the correct zone. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, keep 100 ft from water, no fires, and carry waste out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: One party, and often only a ledge or a gravel patch for two people
